newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Germany pledges global commitment at U.N.
newsitem.headline: Germany pledges global commitment at U.N.

text.p: Germany, pleased that so many countries supported its bid for a permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council, promised on Wednesday it would play a full and responsible role on global issues.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told the General Assembly his country would help with peacekeeping in Bosnia beyond the end of this year, with development in Africa, on European security and on environmental issues.

Many states at the 185-nation annual assembly have supported bids by Germany and Japan to win powerful, veto-carrying seats on the Security Council, joining the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain.

Germany and Japan, the biggest contributors to the U.N. budget after the United States, have been at pains to stress they are now responsible members of the world community and have put the stigma of the Second World War behind them.
The five permanent Security Council members took their positions in 1945 as the victors in the war.

"We are pleased that a large number of member states are in favour of a permanent seat for Germany on the Security Council," Kinkel said. "This, the principal guardian of world peace, still bears the countenance of the year 1945 but it now needs a new one for the year 2000. It is a question of enhancing that body's legitimacy, credibility and effectiveness."

He said the time was approaching for decisions on U.N. reform, but diplomats said this was unlikely soon because there was little agreement on which developing nations should win seats on an expanded Security Council.

Kinkel said the United Nations, in a financial crisis that threatens it with bankruptcy, would have to find still more savings. But he indirectly criticised the United States and other countries that owe the United Nations money.
"The need for reform is no justification for refusing to pay contributions. ... Special rights also imply special duties," he said.

Stressing themes of duty and responsibility, Kinkel outlined many areas where Bonn has a special role to play in global affairs, including in the military sphere, which was once taboo because of Germany's Nazi past.

Germany took in more than 300,000 refugees from the war in Bosnia and was prepared to take part in the NATO-led peace force if its mandate was extended into next year. "Germany is willing to provide her military contribution," Kinkel said.

He also said Bonn supported efforts to integrate Africa, the world's poorest continent, into the global economy through development aid and investment. "Germany will remain a good partner and friend for the nations of Africa."
